I end up terrified that I will lose my financial stability and wind up old, alone, and forced to depend on others.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what specifically happens when you try to engage in social activities or tasks you've been avoiding, and what thoughts or feelings make it difficult for you to follow through?\n\nPatient: When an invitation comes up, I feel so physically exhausted and on edge that I just can't bring myself to go. My mind immediately gets flooded with worries about my finances and retirement, and I feel like I won't be able to focus or be good company anyway. Ultimately, I end up turning them down because I simply don't have the energy to be present with the people I care about.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how long you've been experiencing these overwhelming worries and feelings of being on edge, and was there a specific event or change in your life that you think might have triggered the start of these feelings?\n\nPatient: This constant worrying and tension has been wearing me down for a little over a year now. It really started when my youngest niece left for college and I began seriously contemplating retirement and scaling back my real estate work. Around that same time, the housing market became very volatile, which left me feeling incredibly uncertain about my future income.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that your worries and feelings of being on edge started around the time your niece left for college and you began thinking about retirement and the volatile housing market. Do you think these specific life changes and stressors are directly triggering your current state, or do you feel like your reaction to them is disproportionate to the actual challenges they pose?\n\nPatient: While the housing market and retirement are real concerns, my reaction to them feels completely disproportionate and over-the-top. Even when I tell myself to stop because it’s ridiculous, my mind just spirals into worst-case scenarios like losing my home and ending up alone, which goes far beyond the actual situation.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a typical day and how your worries and physical symptoms, such as exhaustion and tension, affect your ability to perform daily tasks and maintain your usual level of productivity?\n\nPatient: My day starts at 4 AM waking up exhausted with a racing heart, and once I'm at work, my concentration is so poor that I make mistakes like missing contract clauses or forgetting client calls because I'm constantly rereading things. Throughout the day, my neck feels like concrete and I clench my jaw during drives, which leaves me so physically and mentally depleted by evening that I just isolate myself and turn down any social invitations.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant changes in your appetite or weight over the past year, which could be related to your current emotional state?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't noticed any significant changes in my appetite or my weight over the past year. My eating habits have stayed pretty much the same despite all of this stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how often you experience feelings of fatigue or exhaustion without any clear reason or provocation, separate from the times when you're actively worrying about something?\n\nPatient: I don't really experience fatigue or exhaustion without a clear reason. Instead, it always feels directly tied to my poor sleep, the constant worrying, and the physical tension I carry in my body throughout the day.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any specific situations or tasks that you used to handle with ease but now avoid due to feelings of anxiety or being overwhelmed, and how do you think your avoidance of these tasks affects your daily life and relationships?\n\nPatient: I used to manage a busy client load with ease, but now I find myself avoiding or delaying returning client calls on time, which is starting to hurt my professional reputation. I’ve also been turning down social invitations because I feel too exhausted and on edge to be present, which is really straining my relationships with friends and family. It feels like this anxiety is slowly chipping away at both my career and my personal life.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your worries and physical symptoms, such as exhaustion and tension, are more related to your overall feeling of being overwhelmed and fatigued, or are they specifically triggered by your fears and anxieties about the future and losing control?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely driven by my fears of the future and losing control. The physical tension in my shoulders and jaw, as well as my exhaustion, are directly triggered by the constant worst-case scenarios running through my mind about my finances, retirement, and losing my identity as a successful broker. When my mind starts spinning about those fears, my body just reacts to that constant mental strain.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your excessive worry and anxiety are primarily focused on specific aspects of your life, such as work or finances, or do you feel a more general sense of mental and physical exhaustion that interferes with your daily functioning?\n\nPatient: It is really a combination of both; while my worries trigger around specific things like my work, finances, retirement, and my niece, they quickly spiral into uncontrollable worst-case scenarios. This constant mental spinning then causes profound physical and mental exhaustion—including terrible sleep, severe muscle tension, and headaches. Ultimately, this exhaustion is what is actively interfering with my ability to perform at work and maintain my social life."

When my mind starts spinning about those fears, my body just reacts to that constant mental strain.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your excessive worry and anxiety are primarily focused on specific aspects of your life, such as work or finances, or do you feel a more general sense of mental and physical exhaustion that interferes with your daily functioning?\n\nPatient: It is really a combination of both; while my worries trigger around specific things like my work, finances, retirement, and my niece, they quickly spiral into uncontrollable worst-case scenarios. This constant mental spinning then causes profound physical and mental exhaustion—including terrible sleep, severe muscle tension, and headaches. My mind is always running worst-case scenarios, and even when I try to force myself to stop, the worries just chain from one thing to another. Even when I try to slow down, I don't feel peace—I just feel a persistent loss of control.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have experienced significant fatigue or a lack of energy even after getting enough rest, which is not directly related to your worries about the future or losing control?\n\nPatient: I honestly can't remember the last time I got enough rest, because my mind keeps me spinning in bed until one or two in the morning and then jolts me awake by four or five. My fatigue is entirely tied to this severe lack of sleep and the constant mental tension, rather than happening when I am actually well-rested.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if your excessive worry and anxiety significantly improve or lessen when you are actively engaged in tasks or activities, even if those tasks are not necessarily enjoyable or relaxing?"

Around that same time, the housing market became very volatile, which left me feeling incredibly uncertain about my future income.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that your worries and feelings of being on edge started around the time your niece left for college and you began thinking about retirement and the volatile housing market. Do you think these specific life changes and stressors are directly triggering your current state, or do you feel like your reaction to them is disproportionate to the actual challenges they pose?\n\nPatient: While the housing market and retirement are real concerns, my reaction to them feels completely disproportionate and over-the-top. Even when I tell myself to stop because it’s ridiculous, my mind just spirals into worst-case scenarios like losing my home and ending up alone, which goes far beyond the actual situation.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a typical day and how your worries and physical symptoms, such as exhaustion and tension, affect your ability to perform daily tasks and maintain your usual level of productivity?\n\nPatient: My day starts at 4 AM waking up exhausted with a racing heart, and once I'm at work, my concentration is so poor that I make mistakes like missing contract clauses or forgetting client calls because I'm constantly rereading things. Throughout the day, my neck feels like concrete and I clench my jaw during drives, which leaves me so physically and mentally depleted by evening that I just isolate myself and turn down any social invitations.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant changes in your appetite or weight over the past year, which could be related to your current emotional state?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't noticed any significant changes in my appetite or my weight over the past year. My eating habits have stayed pretty much the same despite all of this stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how often you experience feelings of fatigue or exhaustion without any clear reason or provocation, separate from the times when you're actively worrying about something?\n\nPatient: I don't really experience fatigue or exhaustion without a clear reason. Instead, it always feels directly tied to my poor sleep, the constant worrying, and the physical tension I carry in my body throughout the day.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any specific situations or tasks that you used to handle with ease but now avoid due to feelings of anxiety or being overwhelmed, and how do you think your avoidance of these tasks affects your daily life and relationships?\n\nPatient: I used to manage a busy client load with ease, but now I find myself avoiding or delaying returning client calls on time, which is starting to hurt my professional reputation. I’ve also been turning down social invitations because I feel too exhausted and on edge to be present, which is really straining my relationships with friends and family. It feels like this anxiety is slowly chipping away at both my career and my personal life.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your worries and physical symptoms, such as exhaustion and tension, are more related to your overall feeling of being overwhelmed and fatigued, or are they specifically triggered by your fears and anxieties about the future and losing control?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely driven by my fears of the future and losing control. The physical tension in my shoulders and jaw, as well as my exhaustion, are directly triggered by the constant worst-case scenarios running through my mind about my finances, retirement, and losing my identity as a successful broker. When my mind starts spinning about those fears, my body just reacts to that constant mental strain.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your excessive worry and anxiety are primarily focused on specific aspects of your life, such as work or finances, or do you feel a more general sense of mental and physical exhaustion that interferes with your daily functioning?\n\nPatient: It is really a combination of both; while my worries trigger around specific things like my work, finances, retirement, and my niece, they quickly spiral into uncontrollable worst-case scenarios. This constant mental spinning then causes profound physical and mental exhaustion—including terrible sleep, severe muscle tension, and headaches. Ultimately, this exhaustion is what is actively interfering with my ability to perform at work and maintain my social life.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any periods during the day where you feel relatively calm and your mind is not preoccupied with worries, or if the anxiety and feelings of being overwhelmed are constant and unrelenting?\n\nPatient: The anxiety and worry are completely constant and unrelenting throughout the day, with no real periods of calm. My mind is always running worst-case scenarios, and even when I try to force myself to stop, the worries just chain from one thing to another. Even when I try to slow down, I don't feel peace—I just feel a persistent loss of control.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have experienced significant fatigue or a lack of energy even after getting enough rest, which is not directly related to your worries about the future or losing control?\n\nPatient: I honestly can't remember the last time I got enough rest, because my mind keeps me spinning in bed until one or two in the morning and then jolts me awake by four or five. My fatigue is entirely tied to this severe lack of sleep and the constant mental tension, rather than happening when I am actually well-rested.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if your excessive worry and anxiety significantly improve or lessen when you are actively engaged in tasks or activities, even if those tasks are not necessarily enjoyable or relaxing?\n\nPatient: No, keeping busy doesn't actually relieve the anxiety at all. Even though I fill my schedule with work and activities to stay productive, the worry is always running in the background. Even when I am actively trying to focus on tasks like reading contracts, my mind still drifts to worst-case scenarios, causing me to lose my train of thought.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your worries and anxieties are more about specific, identifiable concerns, such as your finances or retirement, or are they more free-floating and not necessarily tied to any specific issue or problem?\n\nPatient: My worries are definitely tied to specific things, like my retirement, my finances, the volatile housing market, and my niece at college. However, these worries don't stay isolated; they quickly chain together and snowball into worst-case scenarios, making it feel like everything is going wrong at once.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned feeling too exhausted and anxious to participate in activities you normally enjoy, but can you tell me if there are any activities that still bring you some sense of pleasure or satisfaction, despite your current state?\n\nPatient: It is really hard to find pleasure or satisfaction in anything right now because my mind is constantly racing and I just feel too exhausted. Even the things I used to do to stay busy, like mentoring younger agents or participating in community events, now just feel like distractions to keep from losing control rather than things that bring genuine satisfaction.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your excessive worry and anxiety patterns have been consistent over the past year, or have there been periods where your symptoms significantly worsened or improved, potentially in response to specific life events or stressors?\n\nPatient: The constant worrying and tension have been pretty consistent and wearing me down for a little over a year now, with no real periods of improvement. It actually started and became much more severe as several major transitions converged all at once: my youngest niece leaving for college, my ex-husband remarrying, and me trying to contemplate retirement in such a volatile housing market.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your anxiety and worry patterns change when you are faced with a situation that you can control versus one that you cannot, and do you find that your reactions to these situations have changed over the past year?\n\nPatient: When I feel in control, I cope by over-scheduling and staying constantly productive, but when faced with things I can't control—like the volatile housing market or my niece moving away—my mind quickly spirals into uncontrollable worries about the future. Over the past year, as these major life transitions piled up, this pattern has become much worse and more exhausting, leaving me feeling like I'm completely losing my grip on my finances and my identity.\n\nDoctor: Can you elaborate on how your need for control, especially in your professional life as a broker, contributes to your anxiety and feelings of being overwhelmed, and do you feel like this need has intensified over the past year with the approaching retirement and changes in the housing market?\n\nPatient: Staying busy and in control of my work has always been my way of feeling secure, but with the volatile housing market and thoughts of retirement, I feel like I'm losing my grip on my finances and my identity. This need for control has definitely intensified over the past year as all these major life transitions converged. It feels like if I slow down for even a moment, everything will fall apart.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your anxiety and worry patterns would change if you were to retire and no longer have the pressures of being a broker, and do you think this would significantly alleviate your feelings of being overwhelmed and losing control?"

One worry just quickly chains into the next, and I can't seem to stop it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your interest or pleasure in activities you normally enjoy, or has your ability to feel happy or satisfied remained the same despite these worries?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about it in terms of losing interest or pleasure. It's more that I feel too exhausted, anxious, and completely overwhelmed to actually participate in or enjoy my usual activities. I just don't have the mental space or energy for them right now.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any physical symptoms like headaches, stomach issues, or difficulty sleeping that seem to coincide with your worries and feeling overwhelmed?\n\nPatient: Yes, my sleep has been terrible; I lie awake until one or two in the morning with my mind spinning, and then wake up early with my heart racing. My neck and shoulders also feel like concrete from tension, and clenching my jaw during drives gives me bad headaches, though I haven't really noticed any stomach issues.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any traumatic events in your past that might be contributing to your current feelings of anxiety and overwhelm?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't experienced any major traumatic events in my past. Nothing of that nature really comes to mind as a trigger for what I'm going through now.\n\nDoctor: Have you found yourself avoiding certain tasks, situations, or places because of your worries or fear of not being able to cope with them?\n\nPatient: Yes, I've been turning down social invitations from my friends and family lately. I just feel too on edge and completely exhausted to cope with socializing or be fully present with them. It feels like I simply don't have the energy to engage with anyone right now.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any feelings of worthlessness, guilt, or hopelessness about your situation or the future?\n\nPatient: No, I wouldn't say I feel worthless or hopeless. It is more that I feel completely overwhelmed by constant worry and a deep fear of losing control over my future, my finances, and my life.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'fear of losing control' and how that fear manifests in your daily life and thoughts?\n\nPatient: My identity and independence are completely tied to being a successful broker, so I try to cope by over-scheduling myself to stay busy and feel in control. But whenever I slow down, my mind immediately spirals into worst-case scenarios, like a single real estate deal falling through leading to me losing my mortgage and my home. I end up terrified that I will lose my financial stability and wind up old, alone, and forced to depend on others.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what specifically happens when you try to engage in social activities or tasks you've been avoiding, and what thoughts or feelings make it difficult for you to follow through?\n\nPatient: When an invitation comes up, I feel so physically exhausted and on edge that I just can't bring myself to go. My mind immediately gets flooded with worries about my finances and retirement, and I feel like I won't be able to focus or be good company anyway. Ultimately, I end up turning them down because I simply don't have the energy to be present with the people I care about.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how long you've been experiencing these overwhelming worries and feelings of being on edge, and was there a specific event or change in your life that you think might have triggered the start of these feelings?\n\nPatient: This constant worrying and tension has been wearing me down for a little over a year now. It really started when my youngest niece left for college and I began seriously contemplating retirement and scaling back my real estate work. Around that same time, the housing market became very volatile, which left me feeling incredibly uncertain about my future income.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that your worries and feelings of being on edge started around the time your niece left for college and you began thinking about retirement and the volatile housing market. Do you think these specific life changes and stressors are directly triggering your current state, or do you feel like your reaction to them is disproportionate to the actual challenges they pose?\n\nPatient: While the housing market and retirement are real concerns, my reaction to them feels completely disproportionate and over-the-top. Even when I tell myself to stop because it’s ridiculous, my mind just spirals into worst-case scenarios like losing my home and ending up alone, which goes far beyond the actual situation.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a typical day and how your worries and physical symptoms, such as exhaustion and tension, affect your ability to perform daily tasks and maintain your usual level of productivity?\n\nPatient: My day starts at 4 AM waking up exhausted with a racing heart, and once I'm at work, my concentration is so poor that I make mistakes like missing contract clauses or forgetting client calls because I'm constantly rereading things. Throughout the day, my neck feels like concrete and I clench my jaw during drives, which leaves me so physically and mentally depleted by evening that I just isolate myself and turn down any social invitations.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant changes in your appetite or weight over the past year, which could be related to your current emotional state?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't noticed any significant changes in my appetite or my weight over the past year. My eating habits have stayed pretty much the same despite all of this stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how often you experience feelings of fatigue or exhaustion without any clear reason or provocation, separate from the times when you're actively worrying about something?\n\nPatient: I don't really experience fatigue or exhaustion without a clear reason. Instead, it always feels directly tied to my poor sleep, the constant worrying, and the physical tension I carry in my body throughout the day.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any specific situations or tasks that you used to handle with ease but now avoid due to feelings of anxiety or being overwhelmed, and how do you think your avoidance of these tasks affects your daily life and relationships?\n\nPatient: I used to manage a busy client load with ease, but now I find myself avoiding or delaying returning client calls on time, which is starting to hurt my professional reputation. I’ve also been turning down social invitations because I feel too exhausted and on edge to be present, which is really straining my relationships with friends and family. It feels like this anxiety is slowly chipping away at both my career and my personal life.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your worries and physical symptoms, such as exhaustion and tension, are more related to your overall feeling of being overwhelmed and fatigued, or are they specifically triggered by your fears and anxieties about the future and losing control?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely driven by my fears of the future and losing control. The physical tension in my shoulders and jaw, as well as my exhaustion, are directly triggered by the constant worst-case scenarios running through my mind about my finances, retirement, and losing my identity as a successful broker. When my mind starts spinning about those fears, my body just reacts to that constant mental strain.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your excessive worry and anxiety are primarily focused on specific aspects of your life, such as work or finances, or do you feel a more general sense of mental and physical exhaustion that interferes with your daily functioning?\n\nPatient: It is really a combination of both; while my worries trigger around specific things like my work, finances, retirement, and my niece, they quickly spiral into uncontrollable worst-case scenarios. This constant mental spinning then causes profound physical and mental exhaustion—including terrible sleep, severe muscle tension, and headaches. Ultimately, this exhaustion is what is actively interfering with my ability to perform at work and maintain my social life.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any periods during the day where you feel relatively calm and your mind is not preoccupied with worries, or if the anxiety and feelings of being overwhelmed are constant and unrelenting?\n\nPatient: The anxiety and worry are completely constant and unrelenting throughout the day, with no real periods of calm. My mind is always running worst-case scenarios, and even when I try to force myself to stop, the worries just chain from one thing to another. Even when I try to slow down, I don't feel peace—I just feel a persistent loss of control.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have experienced significant fatigue or a lack of energy even after getting enough rest, which is not directly related to your worries about the future or losing control?\n\nPatient: I honestly can't remember the last time I got enough rest, because my mind keeps me spinning in bed until one or two in the morning and then jolts me awake by four or five. My fatigue is entirely tied to this severe lack of sleep and the constant mental tension, rather than happening when I am actually well-rested.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if your excessive worry and anxiety significantly improve or lessen when you are actively engaged in tasks or activities, even if those tasks are not necessarily enjoyable or relaxing?\n\nPatient: No, keeping busy doesn't actually relieve the anxiety at all. Even though I fill my schedule with work and activities to stay productive, the worry is always running in the background. Even when I am actively trying to focus on tasks like reading contracts, my mind still drifts to worst-case scenarios, causing me to lose my train of thought.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your worries and anxieties are more about specific, identifiable concerns, such as your finances or retirement, or are they more free-floating and not necessarily tied to any specific issue or problem?\n\nPatient: My worries are definitely tied to specific things, like my retirement, my finances, the volatile housing market, and my niece at college. However, these worries don't stay isolated; they quickly chain together and snowball into worst-case scenarios, making it feel like everything is going wrong at once.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned feeling too exhausted and anxious to participate in activities you normally enjoy, but can you tell me if there are any activities that still bring you some sense of pleasure or satisfaction, despite your current state?\n\nPatient: It is really hard to find pleasure or satisfaction in anything right now because my mind is constantly racing and I just feel too exhausted. Even the things I used to do to stay busy, like mentoring younger agents or participating in community events, now just feel like distractions to keep from losing control rather than things that bring genuine satisfaction.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your excessive worry and anxiety patterns have been consistent over the past year, or have there been periods where your symptoms significantly worsened or improved, potentially in response to specific life events or stressors?\n\nPatient: The constant worrying and tension have been pretty consistent and wearing me down for a little over a year now, with no real periods of improvement. It actually started and became much more severe as several major transitions converged all at once: my youngest niece leaving for college, my ex-husband remarrying, and me trying to contemplate retirement in such a volatile housing market.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your anxiety and worry patterns change when you are faced with a situation that you can control versus one that you cannot, and do you find that your reactions to these situations have changed over the past year?\n\nPatient: When I feel in control, I cope by over-scheduling and staying constantly productive, but when faced with things I can't control—like the volatile housing market or my niece moving away—my mind quickly spirals into uncontrollable worries about the future. Over the past year, as these major life transitions piled up, this pattern has become much worse and more exhausting, leaving me feeling like I'm completely losing my grip on my finances and my identity.\n\nDoctor: Can you elaborate on how your need for control, especially in your professional life as a broker, contributes to your anxiety and feelings of being overwhelmed, and do you feel like this need has intensified over the past year with the approaching retirement and changes in the housing market?\n\nPatient: Staying busy and in control of my work has always been my way of feeling secure, but with the volatile housing market and thoughts of retirement, I feel like I'm losing my grip on my finances and my identity. This need for control has definitely intensified over the past year as all these major life transitions converged. It feels like if I slow down for even a moment, everything will fall apart.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your anxiety and worry patterns would change if you were to retire and no longer have the pressures of being a broker, and do you think this would significantly alleviate your feelings of being overwhelmed and losing control?\n\nPatient: Actually, the thought of retirement triggers more anxiety for me rather than relieving it. I just feel too on edge and completely exhausted to cope with socializing or be fully present with them.
